reason: I'll start with the peripheral nerve route, since sensory information must travel inward from the periphery.
expectation: I expect Schwann cells to wrap the nerve fibres, perhaps forming myelin that supports signal conduction.

alternatives.reason: Building the spinal cord also seems necessary, but I prefer to start at the periphery.

effect: The peripheral nerve is myelinated, so I can now build the central structures needed for the route.
reaction: The wrapped axons and gaps make the nerve's structure clear, though their role isn't explained yet.
reason: The spinal cord is the next central structure along the sensory route.
expectation: I expect to make a spinal cord with central grey matter and surrounding white-matter tracts.

alternatives.reason: The brain is also needed, but the spinal cord comes first along the route.

effect: The spinal cord now provides the central connection for the peripheral nerve.
reaction: The butterfly-shaped grey matter makes the cord's arrangement easy to picture.
reason: I'll connect the peripheral nerve to the spinal cord to continue the sensory route inward.
expectation: I expect a nerve-to-spinal-cord connection carrying sensory signals inward and motor signals outward.

alternatives.reason: The brain is also needed, but connecting the nerve follows the route from the periphery.

effect: The peripheral nerve now connects sensory input and motor output to the spinal cord, with local circuits between them.
reaction: The separate entry and exit routes clarify how fibres can share a nerve.
reason: I'll build the brain so the sensory route can eventually reach it.
expectation: I expect a brain structure combining grey matter with connecting white-matter pathways.

alternatives.reason: Pain input could trace the route into the cord first, but the brain is also needed for the goal.

effect: The brain now has ascending and descending pathways available to connect with the spinal cord.
reaction: The cutaway distinguishes the cerebral outer layer from the underlying pathways, though the cerebellum's role is not explained.
reason: Connecting the brain and spinal cord should complete the central route for sensory information.
expectation: I expect a connected brain and spinal cord with pathways carrying signals between them.

alternatives.reason: Pain input could be followed into the cord now, but I want to connect the route to the brain first.

effect: The brain, spinal cord and peripheral nerves now form a connected model for tracing signals.
reaction: The distinction between connected pathways and a signal's particular destination is useful.
reason: I'll trace touch from the periphery toward the brain to address the sensory goal.
expectation: I expect touch signals to travel through peripheral nerves and spinal pathways toward the brain, though the intermediate connections are unclear.

alternatives.reason: Pain is another sensory route, but I chose touch first.
Cortical motor activity could address the motor goal, but I want to trace sensation first.

effect: Touch activity reaches the cortex through the cord, brainstem and a deep relay, completing the sensory goal.
reaction: The route is clear, though the relay is not named or explained.
reason: I'll trace the cortical motor route to address the remaining goal.
expectation: I expect motor activity to descend from the cortex through the spinal cord to an outgoing motor nerve, though the intermediate connections are unclear.

alternatives.reason: Pain input could lead to the spinal route, but I want to follow the cortical route.

effect: The cortical command reaches a spinal motor neuron and exits along its axon, completing the motor goal; the text also connects this output to the untraced local spinal route.
reaction: The shared final motor neuron is a useful link between the two routes.

mostWorthwhile.text: Connecting the peripheral nerve to the spinal cord was most worthwhile: the planned cross-section distinguishes sensory entry from motor exit while explaining how both share a nerve.

leastWorthwhile.text: The brain construction was less informative: its planned cutaway identifies the cerebellum and brainstem but does not explain their roles.

surprise.text: The descending cortical route and local spinal route can influence the same final motor neurons, linking the two alternatives rather than making them entirely separate outputs.

arbitrary.text: No action felt purposeless, though the deep relay in the touch pathway was unnamed and unexplained, leaving that connection less clear.

continue.text: I would continue to see the spinal route traced and compared with the cortical route; the shared motor neurons make that comparison interesting.
